speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-170, an Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring fishery enterprises, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Hon. Members will note that there are 13 motions on the Notice Paper at report stage of Bill C-170, an Act to authorize investment in and the provision of financial assistance to the Atlantic Fisheries for the purpose of restructuring fishery enterprises.
The Chair is prepared to rule on the procedural acceptability of these motions. However, if need be, the Chair would give an opportunity to Hon. Members who wish to comment at this stage. Perhaps the Chair could be useful to Hon. Members by indicating in a preliminary way the direction in which the ruling will be made.
There are two motions standing in the name of the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) which the Chair is prepared to accept; all other motions the Chair is prepared to reject. However, the Chair will hear any Hon. Member who wishes to contribute to the procedure at this time.

Mr. Speaker, 1 simply want to put the case for the particular amendment which I placed on the Order Paper. It will amend the Bill in order to change the mandate of the Canadian Saltfish Corporation to allow it to become the instrument for the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation.
[DOT]	(1110)
I would simply put to you, Sir, and to the House that this Bill before the House now flows from the Kirby report. Indeed, a recommendation in the Kirby report was the setting up of a Northern Fisheries Development Corporation to administer those plants in the area north of 50 degrees, in northern Newfoundland, on the coast of Labrador and in Quebec.
Kirby examined various options, Mr. Speaker, rejected some and made the recommendation. The Kirby report, which included that recommendation, was approved by the Government of Canada. Indeed, the Government of Canada approved that particular recommendation and, I understand, wants to proceed with that course of action. My point is that this Bill which is before us now gives effect to the recommendations coming out of the Kirby report and, I submit, could very well, and should, give effect to that recommendation of the Kirby task force to create the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation. I submit the relevance of the amendment on those grounds, Mr. Speaker.
1 would further point out that the Northern Fisheries Development Corporation was accepted by both Governments in the restructuring agreement. Both Governments agreed to a Northern Fisheries Development Corporation. Indeed, that was contained in the memorandum of understanding. Therefore, both Governments want to put this into effect.
I would further submit to you, Sir, that if the Governments agree that the Canadian Saltfish Corporation is the vehicle, there will be no other time, I believe, when we can give legislative authority for that in the House of Commons other than now. The reason I submit this amendment now, Mr. Speaker, is that if the Governments want to use the Canadian Saltfish Corporation as a vehicle hereafter, it may be very difficult to permit us to do that in the House of Commons, bearing in mind the legislative timetable after Christmas.
I would further point out to you, Sir, and I would like to put on the record, the concern in the north over this particular vehicle. I have telegrams which I shall not-

On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker. I share the concern of the Hon. Member for the problem he faces in his riding. We have been made aware of his request for an extension of the powers of the corporation and I know from personal experience that in this area of Canada it is
practically impossible for private enterprise to function in a viable, profitable manner. We viewed with some concern the establishment of the corporation in its initial stages and the fact that it was given the right to control all of the saltfishing industry in Atlantic Canada-which is in effect what it ended up to be, the control of the saltfishing industry in Newfoundland. But when it was established it had the effect of putting two of the largest and oldest saltfish companies in my Province of Nova Scotia out of business. This was simply because these companies were in the habit of going to Newfoundland to purchase what we call Labrador slob, bring it back and dry it in the large driers owned by A.M. Smith and Company in Halifax and by Zwicker and Company in my home town of Lunenburg.
The amendment proposed by the Hon. Member seemed to extend the powers of this company. 1 wonder if he has given any thought to impressing upon the Government the necessity of bringing in a separate Bill. The Member stated this was the only opportunity he would have to bring forth changes which would empower the Government to purchase not only salt-fish north of 50, but all other species caught and landed in that area. The concern that we have here is that the amendment proposed by the Hon. Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order, I would simply like to thank the House Leader of the Official Opposition for his intervention and the possibility of an opportunity to debate the substance. I would like to say to you, Sir, that during the second reading debate I laid out before the House my arguments as to why this should take place. I recognize the technical difficulties that you have and the technical difficulties that the House has. As a Member of Parliament I wanted to take advantage of this opportunity, bearing in mind that we do not know when another opportunity will come. How many times have we had fisheries Bills before the House of Commons?
The concern is, Mr. Speaker, that there may be fishermen and plant workers who do not have jobs in the spring. I am concerned about that. I am concerned about plants opening in the spring and about fishermen who are working and are productive in the spring. There is concern in these communities now. Since there is insecurity and uncertainty, people are not investing money and not spending. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Yukon understands that because he represents the north and has lived in the north. He knows what I mean.
I simply want to bring to the attention of the House, governments and the public in general the concern north of 50 for bringing stability, security and certainty to the fishery in that area. If this is not the time-and, of course, I accept your ruling on this amendment-it would at least be a vehicle to bring to the attention of those in the position to do something the necessity to act quickly in order to put those plants in their proper order and to get them working by this spring.
I want to thank Members opposite for their support. I also know there is support on this side of the House, including that of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans who I know supports this in principle and wants to do everything he can to help those people. I want to say again, as I said at second reading, that I appreciate the efforts of the Minister in this whole restructuring effort. I accept your ruling on this, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I wish to thank Hon. Members for their contribution to the procedural matter. I have heard the Hon. Member for Yukon as well. I could perhaps remind him that this period for initial comments,
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
before the Chair makes its ruling, should be taken as an opportunity for Members to make the sort of comments that the Hon. Member for Yukon suggests we do at another time. It would hardly be procedurally acceptable for the Chair to allow debate on motions which it feels are very much out of order and then make the ruling after that debate has taken place. In my opinion, that would create an unacceptable precedent in the conduct of the affairs of the House.
Therefore, I am prepared to rule. Motions No. 10 and 11, standing in the name of the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), are acceptable and should be debated and voted on separately.
Motion No. 12 gives the Chair serious misgivings. All of the other motions in amendment offered by the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) are consequential to Motion No. 12 and therefore I propose to consider them as a group. Motion No. 12 appears to propose an amendment to the Saltfish Act which is not part of the Bill now before the House. As well, the motion infringes upon the financial initiative of the Crown in that it provides for the expenditure of public funds. In fact, the Hon. Member recognizes this in the last section of Motion No. 12. This section does not alter the fact that the amendment infringes on the financial initiative of the Crown, and there are many rulings which confirm that provisions of this kind are not sufficient to make this kind of amendment acceptable.I refer Hon. Members particularly to a ruling by one of my predecessors in a similar case on May 17, 1972, which can be found on page 307 of the Journals.
May I also refer Hon. Members to Citations 540 and 543 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition. Citation 540 states in part:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the Crown is that the communication, to which the Royal Recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of the charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the Crown not only if it increases the amount but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the Crown has demanded or recommended a charge.
Citation 543(1) states:
If any motion or bill or proceeding is offered to be moved, whether in the House or in a committee which requires, but fails to receive, the recommendation of the Crown, it is the duty of the Speaker to announce that no question can be proposed upon the motion, or to direct the withdrawal of the bill, or to say that the problem may be rectified by the proposer obtaining a Royal Recommendation.
Finally, the Hon. Member proposes to add an entirely new proposition to the Bill which is foreign to it, as agreed to at the second reading stage. Such an amendment is quite beyond the scope of the Bill. In this regard, I would refer Hon. Members to Citation 437 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition.
For all these reasons, I must find Motion No. 12 out of order.
As I stated a few moments ago, Hon. Members will realize that Motions Nos. 1 to 9 and Motion No. 13 are consequential

speakeroldname: Mr. Lloyd R. Crouse (South Shore) moved:
speechtext:
That Bill C-170 be amended by adding immediately after line 36 at page 4 the following new clause:
"9. The powers and authority authorized by this Act shall be withdrawn on
a date five years from the proclamation date of this Act unless they have been
re-authorized by Parliament prior to that withdrawal date."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity at report stage to move Motion No. 10 to amend Bill C-170. This amendment is moved in the hope of alleviating the concerns of the representatives of independent companies as well as those put forth by spokesmen of the Governments of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick during hearings at the committee stage with respect to the excessive powers granted to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and the federal Government in this Bill.
If there are any doubts about that statement, I could present literally volumes of documentary evidence as presented to the
marathon sessions of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry hearings which began on Monday morning, November 21, 1983, and which concluded in the wee small hours of Friday morning at approximately 4.30 a.m.
For example, the representatives of the Seafood Processors Association of Prince Edward Island stated, among other things, that the:
-impact and implications of this Bill will be most detrimental-if not, indeed, totally disastrous-to the development or continuance of a viable Atlantic fishery.
A spokesman for the Government of New Brunswick's Fisheries Department asked for the following specific terms, namely:
We would like a guarantee that our fishery will receive a fair share of resource allocation. We would also like to be assured that the restructuring will not interfere with our markets. We are particularly concerned that we are not subjected to a bureaucratic marketing agency that would interpose its bulk between our processors and their customers.
In addition, we would like to participate with the federal Government in a development agreement so that we can continue the innovative, the progressive programs that have assisted the development of our industry, helping it adjust yet again to changing conditions.
The spokesman for the eastern fisheries federation based in Halifax, Nova Scotia presented an excellent brief to the committee. Among other things, he stated: that the Department of Fisheries and the Government in general must be more accountable. Mr. Billard's words:
This Bill leaves absolutely no provision for discussion, debate or review. Bureaucrats will have discretionary powers heretofore unparalleled-
That is his word, "unparalleled".
-in the fishing industry.
He also stated:
If small investors are unable to take risks in the fish processing sector- without fear of government take overs, then there will be no investment. If there are no investments then there will be far fewer fish plants-and that means less fish sold to plants and less competition.
In his view, our fishermen need strong fish processors as much as they need strong fish stocks. 1 am not so sure they need a Government this strong in the fishing industry.
This is the collective voice of the inshore fishermen. For anyone who attended the committee hearings last week, there is no doubt about the almost unanimous voice from the industry and the Provinces expressing the fear that government intervention as authorized by this Bill will not just be a minor aberration in the life of the fishing industry, and that it will not find itself privatized within a few years. Their fear, and it is deeply founded, is that the powers given to this Government will be permanent and, of course, they will be detrimental.
It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I move this amendment in the hope that it will strengthen the Bill and alleviate the fears of the many spokesmen representing literally thousands of plant workers and fishermen who came before our committee throughout the entire period of last week.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments
November 29, 1983

in reply to the amendment of the Hon. Member for South Shore. As he knows, we had a number of days of hearings and in particular very long sessions, one that lasted nearly 20 hours. The Hon. Member is correct when he said many witnesses came before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and indicated a concern that the injection of public capital into the fishing industry did not give rise to a kind of permanent solution to the fishing industry in eastern Canada; that is to say, we would not be taking the first step today toward long-term nationalization.
As the Hon. Member knows, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) had on many occasions publicly as well as on a number of occasions before the committee indicated that that was not our intention. As I said a few days ago, if there are a hundred things the Government could list it wanted to do, injecting capital into the fishing industry would not be one of them. We are there because there really is no alternative.
The Hon. Member will recall that we rejected this amendment in committee because of the idea of saying that on a certain date at a certain time five years hence automatically government authority to be involved in the fishing industry will be dissolved. To suggest that at that particular point in time we would have to sell off our equity would be a very bad business practice, because we would find ourselves advertising to all potential buyers in the marketplace that in approximately three years, on such and such a date, we would be forced by Parliament to sell off the industry and a very good deal by anybody in the market could be had.
I put a question to Mr. Ron Burmer of the Fisheries Council of Canada who appeared before the committee. I said: "From a business point of view, if you were planning on selling an asset, would you predetermine the day and announce it to all potential buyers in the marketplace?" He said: "No". Then I said: "We want to run this on a businesslike basis, so from that point of view would the Government be wise to predetermine a date on which to sell off its assets? Would it not in fact be akin to cherry picking?" Mr. Burner looked at me and said: "Yes, in that circumstance we would all engage in cherry picking"; that is, buying off because we must sell the lucrative pieces that are up for sale, leaving in the hands of the Government those chunks of an industry which do not make money.
1 have a great deal of respect-and i say that sincerely-for the concerns of the Hon. Member that when this industry becomes profitable we privatize it again and get Government out. I also agree wholeheartedly with his concern. However, I disagree that the most appropriate and businesslike way to do it is to predetermine five years down the road a particular day, time and place on which these assets will be disbursed. For that reason we do not support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. 1 wonder whether the Hon. Member who just took his seat could address his comments to my amendment. He failed entirely to do that. I just want to point out to the Chair that the
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
amendment does not mention forced sale or privatization of the assets of any restructured company within a five-year period. The amendment seeks-1 am sorry the Hon. Member either misread its intent or used this period in order to make a strong pitch of his own-to return to Parliament a measure of control over the restructured companies and over the Government.
I point out that the amendment indicates that the powers and authorities authorized by the Act shall be withdrawn on a date five years from the proclamation date of the Act unless they have been reauthorized by Parliament. That is the wording. There is no mention that they must be sold, which the Hon. Member sought to imply. 1 think his comments with regard to the point he raised are valid and there should not be a cut-off date, as he so properly stated. That would simply be a signal sent ahead to everyone to sit back and wait because on day X the axe will fall and all this will be sold. That is not the purpose of the amendment. If the Government finds after five years that it cannot privatize or offer it back to the private sector in that five-year time frame, the amendment seeks to ask the Government to return to Parliament for reauthorization.

speechtext: The Chair is prepared to recognize the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. However, I cannot agree or disagree with the comments of the Hon. Member for South Shore. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I want to acknowledge the fine line of difference which has been drawn by my hon. friend opposite. My comments were made in the vein that the amendment itself arises out of a concern which has been expressed repeatedly that the Government reprivatize the industry.
As to the specific motion, the committee accepted an amendment put by the Hon. Member opposite that the Minister holding the shares of the company be required to report to Parliament once a year on the operations of the new company. It is my contention that that annual report to Parliament meets the concern outlined in the proposed amendment. Again, for that reason we do not support the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to speak very briefly on this subject because when we debated Bill C-170 at second reading 1 spoke at some length on the necessity of imposing a time limitation on the awesome powers of the authorities which are to be granted to the Government pursuant to this Bill. 1 am very pleased the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) was able to

November 29, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act formulate such an amendment as this one. 1 hope it will find favour with the Government.
What we are doing with Bill C-170 is very much the same type of thing we did with the Grand Trunk Railway and other railway companies many years ago when we established Canadian National, something into which Parliament was very much forced. It did not really want to do that, but things got to such a sad and sorry state in the railway business that it became a necessity. Such is the case with the East Coast fishery. If I might paraphrase the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson), he said that the so-called solution proposed in Bill C-170 was probably the least bad of many poor options. As was said by the Hon. Member for South Shore, it gives unparalleled power to the Government, awesome and unparalleled power, which we know will be delegated to the bureaucracy because the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane), who is present today, is unable to keep day to day control over these matters. Therefore his authority over these matters must be delegated to the people on his staff.
At the hearings of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, every representation indicated distrust of government on the part of people in the fishery business. No one appeared to be more distrustful of government than fishermen themselves, as represented through their unions. Normally we can expect unions to be of a more socialist frame of mind than perhaps the majority of the population, but in this case it appeared that the people who make their livelihood on fishing vessels or in fish plants more than anyone else were distrustful of government and wanted to see a time limit placed on the authorities we were to give to government.
One problem with which we in the House are faced is that whenever we establish a new governmental institution, a new department or branch of government, a Crown corporation or any other entity, the entity always sees its first order of priority as being able to maintain itself. Also, it is very difficult to get rid of such an entity. There is always a problem with dismantling government institutions. If we pass this amendment and it becomes part of the law, there will be an incentive right from its inception for the people concerned with the new institutions, because just a few years down the road the Government will have to set aside its powers and authorities and we will of necessity have to put the fishing business back in private hands where it rightfully belongs.
I disagree with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Tobin) who said that having a set determination date will be a major impediment if assets are to be sold at the end of that period. I do not disagree with him entirely when he says that this will naturally flow from the motion, because surely the idea is to dispose of the assets that will be owned by these new companies and get them into private hands. There might be some difficulty with that, but 1 do not think it is an overriding difficulty. That it will be necessary for people involved in the new fish companies to begin planning a
system of privatization right from the start will, 1 think, work to the benefit of the East Coast fisheries.
If all else fails, Sir, my colleague, the Hon. Member for South Shore, has included in his amendment the concept that the Government can come back to Parliament and ask for an extension of that five-year period. If improvements have not been made and if there is real difficulty disposing of the assets into private hands, that option is always available to the Government. However, it does mean that Parliament will again have to look at the situation and approve any possible extension.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), but I would have liked to see it provide for a period of less than five years. The purpose of this Bill is simply to restructure the two super companies. The agreement the Government has reached with the Province of Newfoundland, according to the letter submitted by Dr. Kirby to the Bank of Nova Scotia, provides that at the end of a ten-year period the bank may offer the shares to the Government and the Government will have to purchase at par the Class A preferred shares which are then held by the bank in Holding Company "Y".
Once those two super companies are restructured and once the Quebec Pecheurs Unis is restructured, I do not see that there is a need for the continuation of the Bill. First, the $100 million which has been guaranteed in the Bill must be approved by Parliament in the future. It must be included in the estimates. That could be done under another program or through the Department of Fisheries.
That would happen if the development program designed to aid the small processors we have heard about, which is a part of the agreement to co-operate between Nova Scotia and the federal Government, comes under that part of the Bill? Once that agreement is arranged, only then will we know how that developmental program will help the small independents. I agree with Mr. Crouse when he says that those small independents came before us last week and told us that Newfoundland independents are protected by $12 million worth of guarantees from the Province of Newfoundland. In Quebec, the Pecheurs Unis is being nationalized. The Government will not touch the rest of the independents but has made an offer of assistance to them for upgrading and modernization in the amount, I am told, of 60 per cent.
Under this Bill or in the arrangement made between the Government and the Province of Newfoundland, there has been nothing given to independent processors from Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That was a concern we heard from independents like Fishpac and from the exporters group who asked us what would happen to them and who would they have to deal with in order to accomplish the $400 million worth of sales that we were told about.
I agree with Mr. Crouse about the duration of the powers of this Bill. I have concern with the fact that written into the agreements will be the enterprise allocations for fish for these
November 29, 1983

two super companies. The companies that will now be restructured had for the last two years an enterprise allocation. However, in my view what will hurt the inshore fishery even more is the percentages of those enterprise allocations which will be written into the agreements for the next five-year period. The Minister shall dispose of such portion of any interest in a fishery enterprise-

I throw that suggestion out to let you know, sir, that there will be agreement on this side if she wishes to amend my amendment to two or three years. We would accept that subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that there is conflict in this amendment, just from the point of view of having chaired the committee, if we limit the restructuring of these two super companies to one year. I personally feel that the Bill will be around a lot longer, because in Nova Scotia we do not know what the time frame will be. We are told it will be five years. In Newfoundland, we definitely know that the bank, which would not appear before the committee, is tied in to not receiving any of the 5 per cent for ten years. I guess what I am saying is that I agree with and support the suggestion that there should be a limitation, but on the other side of the

November 29, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act question the negotiations and the Bill itself have already set it beyond five years.
As to the other concerns, I certainly questioned the Minister of Fisheries for Nova Scotia as to the enterprise allocation when he was before the committee on Thursday night, and as well I questioned the independents. The Nova Scotia Deputy Minister said that he would be in favour of a percentage of the enterprise allocation being incorporated in the agreement. I am not sure that tomorrow's meeting in Montreal on AGAC will not do that, even though there is opposition from the weaker sector, the inshore fishery.
As for the independents, I certainly mentioned and questioned them on several occasions and specifically questioned the Nova Scotia Minister of Fisheries, who said that the independents in Nova Scotia-and he referred to the Hon. Member for South Shore-were independent and that no one had come to him. I question that because I know of two cases in South West Nova who feel, regardless of this Bill, that there would be nothing for them in guarantees from either the Province of Nova Scotia, as in Newfoundland with regard to the $12 million, or from the federal Government.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the support for the concept of a sunset clause in this Bill. I have to tell the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) that this does not in any way interfere with the ten-year arrangement which may have been made with the banks; or at least, if it does interfere in any way, it is not an insoluble situation. If the Government does what it says it would strive to do, namely dispose of the structure to private enterprise, that undertaking should be incorporated in any agreement with private enterprise. The Government or the purchasers would then become responsible for such residual portion of outstanding debt to the bank as might exist.
I do not see any conflict between that and a five-year term for the Bill, with renewal if necessary. My experience in the House has been that if a logical case can be made that something is to the detriment of the Canadian economy in general and the Atlantic fishery in particular, the House would co-operate in the extension of time. So I do not share the Hon. Member's concern about the ten-year clause in the agreement.
I come from a constituency which the local office of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in New Brunswick advises me has 3,000 people who are dependent for full-time or part-time employment on the processing industry in the Bay of Fundy area. Probably half that number depend on the industry for full-time employment and the other half depend on it for part-time employment to supplement their other income.
This is, then, a matter of major concern to me and to my constituents. There is not a single plant that is to be operated under the nationalization structure and I am happy about that. What I am really concerned about when I see the agreements that have been made, which include the transfer of part of the scallop fleet from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland, are the constraints that may be imposed on the inshore fishermen. In this, my concerns are parallel with those of the Hon. Member
for South West Nova. Fishermen and their employees are concerned about their futures should this occur.
The greatest problem is that there was no consultation in the Fisheries Committee and there was no consultation with Government. As a result of consultation within the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, a conclusion was reached which was the only solution offered to resolve the very serious social problem of unemployment.
The search for a solution to this social problem does not address the long-run consequences which may be suffered from the nationalization of this industry. This emphasizes the necessity for such an industry to operate under a syndicated directorate, under a creditors' management proposition, or any other proposition which would allow it to enter world markets in a relatively independent and free enterprise structure.
As I have said before in debate on this Bill, I doubt very much if there is any capability in the structures of Canada which can equal the marketing capabilities of the fish processing structures in Atlantic Canada. But we are going to lose those marketing capabilities, or if we do not lose them totally we are going to put them under the direction of people who may not be familiar with the process. We cannot allow this to happen any more than we can sell potatoes to 100 countries over a period of time, meet the quality requirements and make the decisions which have to be made over the telephone. That is the question which I raised in committee. I would like to see this Bill have a sunset date. I see no problem of renewing it in the House of Commons if and when an urgency arises which does demand that extension.
I am concerned that there is an opportunity for the Government to have controlling shares in both intergovernmental arrangements for the operation of the fisheries in the two Maritime Provinces of Canada. I believe that there should be an element of balance between the fishery people themselves, the provincial Government and the Government of Canada in the distribution of voting shares in that company. The Government of Canada will find itself in a very serious conflict of interest-no matter who may be the Minister who heads the corporation-when it has at its disposal the allocation of quotas, the enterprise allocation, which has been a proposition and a partial policy of government, and all the other aspects of regulations and licensing over which it has control, while at the same time managing the sale of fisheries. There are the representations which were made to that committee in all sincerity, asking the Government do not put itself in a position of conflict of interest.
There is within this Bill the capability of loaning $100 million to the fishing industry. However, when the Minister and his staff were asked if this money in fact would be available to independents who found themselves in a difficult financial position, it was not positively addressed by either the Minister or his staff. If at this date the Minister wishes to address that question and say "Yes, in small bites when necessary, there will in fact be prompt consideration given to
November 29, 1983

the application of an independent for a loan as guaranteed under this Act", it would put somewhat of a different light on the position the independents would occupy in the presence of the elephantine-sized structure which is being put in place under public control.
By all means, Mr. Speaker, let us give favourable consideration to this amendment which does nothing to the principle of the Bill. It does nothing to contradict the objectives of the Government, as outlined by the Minister and his staff. What it does do, however, is give an element of confidence to the other people in the fishing industry that perhaps somewhere down the line business may return to normal. 1 think that is important. 1 believe the independents would then feel they could hang on, perhaps for five years, if there were guaranteed loans from the Government to replace their credit destroyed by virtue of the bank attitude toward this structure.
These things have to be resolved. If we were contradicting the Bill by this amendment, I would say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it would deserve to be rejected, and so would the independents who asked for a sunset clause. But we are not. We do not have any opportunity really to interfere in the management of the structure for, let us say, four-plus years if there is a five-year sunset clause as this amendment suggests. It does not hamper the Government and I believe it would indicate to fishermen and to this House that the Government has the same spirit of understanding and co-operation which existed throughout the committee hearings. There was no political confrontation in those committee meetings per se. There was, in fact, the presentation of the facts as the witnesses saw them. They were given open consideration by virtually every member of the committee. Only when one tried to offer amendments which would represent the presentations of the witnesses did we seem to break on party lines.
1 believe the remarks of the Hon. Member for South West Nova are indicative of the spirit in which that Bill was in fact discussed in committee. I wish it could be discussed in this House in the same spirit and with the same objectives in mind, namely, the wellbeing of the fishing industry as a whole. The objectives should not be the wellbeing of the Crown Corporation, but the wellbeing of the private enterprise structure, which has served us so well and which has remained afloat financially in hard times.
We should consider as well those who had exaggerated expectations which were never realized and, therefore, ended up in a position of bankruptcy. Let us consider them all in the generosity of spirit which I believe is intended in this Bill as it addresses the fishing industry. Let us not be divided on strictly partisan terms, but be together for the greater benefit of the fishing industry of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by saying that this is the first opportunity I have had to address the House on the matter of Bill C-170, an Act to restructure the Atlantic fishery. I recognize that at this point we are dealing with a very narrow issue, in particular the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). At the same time I believe we have
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
to consider that amendment in the context of the total provisions of the Bill and the background against which the Bill was promoted by the Government and introduced in this House by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane).
Let me say, first of all, with respect to the amendment that I feel it is simply an honest attempt by a Member of Parliament, who has had vast experience in the fisheries as well as in the House of Commons, to provide a safety valve to those who are concerned and suspicious about the implementation of the provisions of this Bill. 1 see no need to view with any degree of suspicion the motives of those who would support this amendment, because their motives are quite obvious. It provides and ensures that at some future point the provisions of this Bill will be reviewed, not at the request of anyone, not at the demand of persons who are injured or adversely affected by the provisions of the Bill, but as of right in the normal course of parliamentary processes.
That is what this sunset provision is all about, Mr. Speaker. It simply allows and ensures that the sun will not set once and for all on the provisions of this Bill, but that the provisions will again, at some future point, be re-examined and reviewed by the Chamber responsible for the enactment of the Bill, the House of Commons. I believe that is an obligation which we ought to impose upon ourselves to satisfy those who are justly concerned about the potential adverse effect of this Bill.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that we must consider this amendment in the context of what has gone on before. I want to review very briefly the background to Bill C-170, an Act to provide for the restructuring of the Atlantic fishery. We were first informed of the actions of the Government with respect to the Atlantic fishery in January of 1982. At that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the formation of the Task Force on Atlantic Fisheries and indicated that one, Mr. Michael J. L. Kirby, would act as chairman of the task force. The press release which accompanied that announcement gave a very clear indication of what Mr. Kirby's task was and what he was to do, and underlined the fact that there was an urgency involved in the process. In fact, the release under the hand of the Prime Minister said that the task force was to proceed on an urgent basis to review the Government's policies and regulations which affected the fishery. It was also to consider the social context of the Atlantic fishery, particularly the concern of people in the Maritime Provinces and the Province of Newfoundland over the loss of employment which was being experienced because of disruptions in the fishing industry.
In December of 1982, that same year, we were asking in the House of Commons when we would receive the report of the task force, which was presumably given urgent priority by the Government. My colleague, the Hon. Member for South Shore, as well as myself, asked on occasion when we would receive the report. We were receiving a report by what was termed a "trial balloon". Mr. Kirby and the members of his task force on the Atlantic fisheries kept leaking out the things which they were considering doing. They were going to nationalize the fishing industry. Each time one of these trial balloons went up, the people concerned were faced with the prospect of

November 29, 1983
Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
a dramatic and drastic change in the conduct of the fishing industry. They were faced with that possibility for over 12 months.
Finally, in February, 1983, approximately 14 months after the institution of the task force, its report was made public. Since that time the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada has reviewed very carefully the recommendations in the report. Much argument and discussion was generated. But when the Government finally made its decision with respect to the implementation of the report, as represented by Bill C-170, we have something very much different from the original recommendations, something which has caused elements of the Atlantic fishery great concern for their future.
The independent operators in the Atlantic fishery look at the provisions of Bill C-170 and see no assistance for them. On the contrary, there is relatively massive assistance for their major competitors, the large corporations which will be rolled into an even larger corporation in the case of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. So it is not hard to realize that after months of consideration, months of rumours and speculation, they are now faced with a Bill which does not give any real indication of what will transpire in the future.
Therefore we must ask ourselves if the independent operators and others engaged in the Atlantic fishery have a legitimate concern? The answer comes back very quickly that yes, they certainly do. In particular, the independent operators in Nova Scotia have no reason to believe that six months, one, two or three years from now they will be able to operate the businesses they have successfully operated in the past. They have no reason to believe the Government will protect them from events which will be damaging to their fishing operations. All they can do is wait and see what happens, how this Bill is implemented by the Government, and how they are affected.
All they ask us to do, Mr. Speaker, is to assure them of a future review of this legislation, which is the purpose of the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for South Shore. It is difficult for me to understand how anyone in this House of Commons who has the vaguest familiarity with the Atlantic fisheries could deny them that opportunity. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask all Members of this House on both sides to show some real concern for the future of those now engaged in the fishing industry and provide in the legislation the right to have their situation reviewed at some future point.
In closing, I simply want again to underline that this is a very legitimate concern of those engaged in the Atlantic fishery. Their future is in jeopardy and they want the assurance that at some future point the whole matter will be reviewed. No one can deny them that right, and the only way to implement that right is through the provision which my colleague from South Shore has proposed be added to Bill C-170.

speechtext:
That Bill C-170, be amended by adding immediately after line 6 at page 5 the following new Clause:
"10.(1) The Auditor General of Canada shall have unlimited access to financial records, accounts, and other documents pertaining to fishery enterprises in which the Government of Canada has more than 49 per cent controlling interest.
(2) The Auditor General shall report only on the expenditure of public funds by enterprises referred to in subsection (1) of this clause, and shall have due regard for the confidentiality of all other information about such enterprises that does not pertain directly to the expenditure of public funds."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the second amendment, No. 11 on the Order Paper, will give the Auditor General access to the accounts of any fishery enterprise in which the federal Government has more than 49 per cent controlling interest. In order to protect the interest of private investors in such enterprises, the Auditor General would report only on the expenditure of public funds by the companies.
Apart from the general argument for accountability, this provision would also act as a deterrent to fishing firms accepting more federal assistance than they strictly need. We have been aware from time to time, from studying various agreements, that sometimes more is asked for than is required. This is true of Government Departments. We learn at the end of sessions that there is a carryover simply because the Department has asked for more money than it actually needed.
This is my concern with regard to this particular piece of legislation. 1 realize that no one actually likes to see the Auditor General coming into their office, but he is the appointed watchdog over the treasury. In our view, once the Government of Canada becomes involved beyond the 50 per cent level in any particular company, there should be some safeguard for the taxpayers of Canada.
There is yet another concern embodied in the so-called secret letter of June 24.

Those of us who served on the committee are aware that early in the committee sessions, I believe it was on Tuesday morning, I requested the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to place before the committee the letter of agreement between the Government of Canada and the Bank of Nova Scotia which spelled out, in some considerable detail, the actual commitment which has been made by the federal Government to the Bank of Nova Scotia, a commitment which many independents referred to as a bailout of the bank. There were many independents who said the bank should have taken its own bath. No one forced them to make these loans. They did it with the hope of securing gain from the interest involved.
If you, Sir, make a bad investment, you have to suffer the loss. In this case the Bank of Nova Scotia obviously made what appears to be a bad investment. They overreached. They overreacted to the 200-mile limit and the euphoria that went with it. They thought there would be no end. They thought everything would keep going up and nothing would ever come down. But in this case things did come down. Here we have the Government of Canada coming in and bailing out, not necessarily the companies, but the Bank of Nova Scotia.

Coming back to what I was saying about the secret letter, the Minister at that time refused to table it. It would have been very helpful. It was only in the late hours of Thursday evening that we were able to obtain the document to which I have referred. I hold it in my hand. It was provided eventually,

as I say, by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is part of the cause of the fears of independents, part of the cause of the concerns of those who are still trying to make a living in the fishing industry.

John Leefe, Minister of Fisheries for the Province of Nova Scotia, appeared and gave his views as they applied to the restructuring industry.

(b) in Holdco Y these shares will carry a 5 per cent cumulative dividend payable at the end of ten years in Class A Preferred Shares.

If one party only wishes to cause Holdco X to hold its assets beyond five years, that party shall have the right to purchase the other party's shares in Holdco X for an aggregate amount equal to the amount which the other party would have received had the assets been sold and a distribution made in accordance with clause 8.
There is much more, but this is the very basis of the over-all restructuring agreement. It is all embodied in this letter. This is the point of debate between the Province of Nova Scotia and the federal Government, as I understand it, Sir. It is one of the requirements of the Government of Nova Scotia that no government or combination of governments shall hold more than 49 per cent of the restructured companies. That was initially agreed to by the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, as 1 understand it, when consultations were held at Port Hawkes-bury in early September. For some unknown reason, these conditions are now to be withdrawn by the federal Government. They are not being met. One of the conditions put forward by the Government of Nova Scotia is that they must be met. However, it is obvious after we read this letter that the federal Government cannot meet that particular condition because they have stated, and I repeat:
At the end of the ten year period, the Bank may offer, and the Government of Canada will purchase at par,-

Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act
They do not say "may" but "will".
There are a number of other reasons which I will quickly put on the record. There are some measures pertaining to accountability and control that should be considered as priority areas. These would include requiring that all funds used under the Act be voted on under the normal appropriation process. It would require an annual report of the operation of the Act, to be tabled no later than, say, two months after the end of the fiscal year. The appropriate parliamentary committee could then review the operations of the restructured companies. A sunset clause should be provided. There should be measures to ensure that nationalized enterprises do not become mini versions of Canadair. There should be some sort of control mechanism with respect to the "public interest" clause. Does the Government of Canada, for example, really need to be exempt from the Combines Investigation Act?
All of these, Mr. Speaker, are concerns of the independent companies and of the fishermen. I put them on the record so that you will realize the basis upon which our motion is moved. I hope it will be acceptable to the Government of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to respond to the Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) and to the amendment which he has proposed to Bill C-170. To be clear, let me say that we on this side of the House do not support the amendment as proposed for a number of reasons.
The first reason is that this amendment, as it now stands, is ultra vires in the case of the agreement that has been reached with the Government of Newfoundland. That is, under the agreement with the Government of Newfoundland the company which will be set up is going to be set up under the Corporation Act of the Province of Newfoundland. This agreement would therefore be ultra vires. That presents a serious problem in itself.
In addition to that problem of legality, the amendment coming at this stage of the game, after an agreement has been reached with Newfoundland, could possibly, in the view of Newfoundland, abrogate an agreement that has already been reached.
The third point I would make is that this amendment, being imposed at this stage on what I would call a piece of enabling legislation, could in theory-I am not saying it would, but could-intrude upon negotiations not yet completed with the Government of Nova Scotia.
The fourth point, Mr. Speaker, is that this amendment, if accepted, would set a precedent as far as Crown corporations are concerned. According to the Financial Administration Act, Crown corporations are scheduled and the Auditor General does not have access in this way for all Crown corporations scheduled D and below. In fact, this particular quasi-Crown corporation, since the Government of Canada will hold shares in the company, would be a schedule E company. It is the intent of the Government to come before the House with a comprehensive policy under the Financial Administration Act as far as Crown corporations are concerned, in accordance
with the suggestion that the Auditor General be given power to examine the books of the company in which the Government holds shares.
Another most important point is that the Government of Canada is not going to own the fishing industry of eastern Canada lock, stock and barrel. As I said earlier, like the Governments of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, since the federal Government really has no other choice it is injecting capital into an industry, through equity, which otherwise would collapse. We know what the ramifications of a collapse would be.
As a result of the Government having 49 per cent of the voting shares, this amendment suggests that the other 51 per cent, or perhaps 60 per cent in the case of Nova Scotia, of the shares held by private entrepreneurs would mean that private entrepreneurs would have their shares and financial statements subject to the scrutiny of the Auditor General of Canada. It would be an incredible precedent to have that private capital subject to scrutiny by the Auditor General. There is no precedent anywhere for that kind of intrusion into the affairs of private business.
I asked Mr. Ron Bulmer, the Fisheries Council of Canada representative who speaks for the processors of Canada, what he thought of this amendment. His response was that it would set a very dangerous precedent if the Government were serious in saying that it was putting in money now through equity capital and wishes to reprivatize when the industry is sound again. If part of the process of reprivatizing the industry is to sell it off in pieces, there are very few people who will want to buy into something which will automatically expose their books and business dealings to the Auditor General of Canada.
For all of those reasons, not the least of which is that it is ultra vires, we cannot accept this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, in my view this amendment is absolutely essential. I do not buy any of the arguments advanced by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Tobin).
If we were to establish a precedent that federal Crown corporations be subject to the scrutiny of the Auditor General, then in my view that would be a good precedent. One of the problems that we have in this country is that Crown corporations are not subject to that scrutiny.
Just let us examine what happened with Canadair. It came back year after year for a period of three or four years and presented figures to the parliamentary committee that was studying it. These figures, presumably from audited statements done by the auditor of their choice, showed that that company was sound. In the third or fourth year we find that it needs an injection of $1.5 billion in taxpayer's money after it had assured us that it was operating soundly. This is what occurs when the Auditor General of Canada, who is responsible to the House, does not have the authority to review the books of Crown corporations.
November 29, 1983

BROADCAST NEWS-DISMISSAL OF BROADCASTING REPRESENTATIVES FROM BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House and Hon. Members on all sides a recent development which again demonstrates in the most shocking manner the cavalier and even dangerous attitude of major Canadian news publishing interests. While this event took place several weeks ago, it received little if any press coverage until today. Yet its implications, and the attitude which it demonstrates, would certainly have been frontpage news were it involving any other enterprise with a similar impact upon Canadian life.
Late in October at a meeting of the Board of Directors of Broadcast News, the subsidiary of Canadian Press, as a result of a conflict between the broadcasting representatives and the publishing representatives, the publishers used their strength to fire all the broadcasting representatives on the Board. The senior manager of Broadcast News was fired by the publishing interests as well. This means that while Canadian television and radio broadcasting interests contribute the largest portion of the funds which run Canadian Press and Broadcast News, the important Broadcast News division, by far the largest domestic news service to Canadian broadcasting interests, has no broadcasting representatives on its Board. They dared to disagree with the publishers. Surely this arrogance and insensitivity by the publishers' representatives is a further warning that, in the news publishing industry in Canada, with all its immense clout, there is shocking insensitivity to the need for broad and diverse input to assure a free press.

subtopic: LOCATION OF STATION IN SICAMOUS, B.C.
LOCATION OF STATION IN SICAMOUS, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would someone construct a covered stadium yet fail to provide any spectator seating? Would someone build a school and forget to instal student desks? Of course not, yet something of this nature is precisely what VIA Rail has done in Sicamous, British Columbia.
Sicamous depends upon VIA Rail for much of its tourist business, as well as for general transportation purposes. However, whenVIA recently constructed a new passenger station in Sicamous it failed to provide any passenger access. An appropriate right-of-way to the station was never obtained, so the station is cut off from public access. As well, the station which is located in the British Columbia snowbelt is open to the harsh winter conditions of the area. It is unheated, unlighted, and has no washroom or toilet facilities. It has no telephones, and there is no way of determining if the arrival of a train is imminent. The station also lacks a parking lot. To call it a station or passenger depot is to use the term very loosely.
The people of Sicamous, British Columbia, hear and read of the Government's commitment to improving western rail transportation, yet are forced to accept a most appalling situation when it comes to VIA Rail service. The people of Sicamous need and support VIA Rail, so I would urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) to intervene in this fiasco and provide the people of Sicamous, British Columbia, with the passenger service they need and deserve.

Order Paper of this session, in the hope that the Government will carry them over and place them on the Order Paper in the upcoming session in the same position that they now enjoy on the Order Paper.
Of course, my first concern has to be with the seven outstanding reports of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. We would not like to see those reports die. We would like to see them resume their position on the Order Paper in the same place they are now.
The same would apply to Bill C-12, the Bill with respect to bankruptcies which has been hanging around now for some eight years and has gone through a substantial portion of the parliamentary machinery this session. We would like to see that Bill restored to the Order Paper in the same position in the forthcoming session as it now enjoys.
The same also applies to Bill C-653 with respect to the Government's intentions, as I understand them, to incorporate the sentiments expressed in Bill C-653 in Bill C-12.
The Committee on Pension Reform has been sitting and has done considerable work. It would be a shame to see that die with the death of this session. We would like to see an order of the House which would ensure that all of the evidence taken by that Committee would find a place on the Order Paper in the same position in the next session as it enjoys now.
November 29, 1983

The same sentiments apply to the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration since that Committee has done a good deal of work which should not die.
Likewise, the Joint Committee on Senate Reform has done a good deal of work and collected a lot of evidence which should carry on in the next session in the same position it is in now so that the work of the Committee is not lost.
The same sentiments apply to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments. There are several reports on the Order Paper now awaiting motions to concur. We believe that those motions should also find their way on to the Order Paper immediately upon the commencement of the new session so that that work is not lost.
The work and the several reports of the Public Accounts Committee should not die. As the Government House Leader knows, those reports indeed go back to 1978. Surely they should be restored and hopefully dealt with in whatever time remains in the next full session of the House.
There may be others that I have not mentioned and which the Government wants to see take their place on the Order Paper in the same position as they enjoy now. Likewise, there may be some work of the House now on the Order Paper that the New Democratic Party might wish to see on the Order Paper in the next session. I would suggest, in order that we might come to some agreement before prorogation tomorrow, that perhaps a House Leaders' meeting be held some time today to reach some common ground on these matters. Second thing, no, we do not agree that they should appear on the Order Paper at the stage where they are now because the Opposition wants to use them as a means to filibuster, whereas we consider that parliamentary reform is too important and that, as can be seen on today's Order Paper, there should not be 200 notices of motions to use as dilatory tactics. On the other hand, I have offered-and the offer stands-to my colleagues of the Opposition to reinstate those reports on the Order Paper under Government Business. If that is not necessary, if they agree to that, good! If they do not agree, too bad!
Second, Bill C-12 is a good suggestion. We will wait for the answer of the New Democratic Party, but that can be settled early in the new session and there is no need to move a motion in this session.
Third, if Bill C-153 is not necessary in this session, we will consider it in the new session.
Fourth, the Committee on Pension Reform is a special Committee, and I understand that a report will be tabled in a few minutes.
Fifth, we do not have to be concerned about the report of the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration in this session because it originates from a standing committee. We can very well consider it at the beginning of the new session.
Sixth, concerning the Joint Committee on Senate Reform, I have been advised that a report will be tabled in a few minutes.
Seventh, about the Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, the answer is no.

Eighth, with respect to the reports of the Committee on Public Accounts, the answer is no. On the subject of finance, since my colleague has asked me a question-
The Hon. Member raised the question of finance. Mr. Speaker, with respect to the matter of the Bill to implement the Ways and Means resolution now on the Order Paper, the income tax Bill, I thank the Government
House Leader for his courtesy. Since the Ways and Means motion itself sets forth verbatim exactly what the Bill will contain, his courtesy in giving us that Ways and Means motion is ample notice to us and we will expect the Bill itself immediately the new session comes along. With respect to any consent necessary to dispense with Standing Orders, we can meet that problem when it arises.
I really deeply regret the decision of the Government House Leader not to restore on the Order Paper the several motions to concur in the reports of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, just as I deeply regret the Government's decision not to restore on the Order Paper the reports of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. He and I take a different view with respect to the process that applies to the life of these reports on prorogation. Under our practices here those reports and all of the evidence will die with prorogation. The Government House Leader shakes his head in the negative. He says that the reports are in the public domain. Sure, they are in the public domain. They are on the library shelf, but unless the Government decides to bring them back into the House there is nothing that Members of the House can do about them.
That applies with equal force to the decision of the Government not to allow the reports of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure to resume the same position which they now enjoy on the Order Paper. What the Government is suggesting when it says it is prepared to bring the reports back but only as Government business-only as Government Orders-is that the Opposition will not have any right to exercise the privilege of moving concurrence if that is what they wish to do. The decision will rest entirely with the Government as to whether any of these reports, and there are seven outstanding, will be adopted. That is not the spirit of reform, particularly not when we have seven excellent, outstanding reports produced by a committee with absolute unanimity on the part of all three Parties. Now the Government wants to put those reports under Government Orders, that being the only condition on which the Government will restore them to the Order Paper. That seems to me to destroy the kind of impartial approach which members of that committee took with respect to the question of reform. The reports should be restored and they should be restored as they are now.
All of the motions to concur which are set down were set down, not for the purpose of obstructing, if that is the Government House Leader's idea, but because of an unfavourable ruling of the Chair, which I do not criticize at this time, with respect to the right of a Member of the House who is present to move concurrence in a report standing by way of a motion in the name of another Member who is absent. That is the reason for the duplication and it is the kind of situation we get into when we are confronted with that kind of ruling, which 1 do not criticize. All of those 74 pages of Members' names would not be on the Order Paper had the ruling been, as 1 thought it should have been at the time, to follow previous practices of the House as they are followed in other instances.
November 29, 1983

1 welcome a House Leaders' meeting this afternoon to discuss these matters in the hope that we can get the Government House Leader to reconsider these matters, particularly in view of all of the years of work that have gone into all of these reports which will go down the tube with prorogation unless they are restored to the Order Paper immediately upon resumption of a new session.

Mr. Speaker, the reports of the parliamentary reform committee do not die. They are in the public domain, they are known, and they may be and will be used in total or in part in the future. That could be in the next session. It is not necessary for them to appear on the Order Paper in the new session. Nevertheless, I have proposed to the Opposition that we allow these reports to be printed on the Order Paper in the new session under Government business, because there is absolutely no way we would allow those reports, on which there are 200 notices of motions, to be put before Government business every day. We went through the sad experience of seeing the Official Opposition using those important reports on parliamentary reform during the Crow debate for the purpose of delay. We will not accept the use of parliamentary reform in the future to delay again.
We want parliamentary reform to take place. We are conducting now a major experiment. We are negotiating some fine tuning of the experiment. My colleagues, the House Leaders, know that very well. We are even using some of the dispositions included in the additional reports for the purpose of fine tuning in the midst of our negotiations. However, there is no way we will allow the Opposition to have the freedom to move concurrence in those reports 200 times before we reach Government business in the new session. It is absolutely unnecessary because the reports will always be useful and will be used in the future. We are suggesting that they be put on the Order Paper under the control of the Government. It is the responsibility of the Government to establish the Order of the Day

November 29, 1983
Business of the House
every day in the House of Commons. I am sure that my colleagues opposite know and understand what I am saying.
To say that we are not interested in those reports is wrong. On the contrary, we think they are most important. We have accepted the ongoing experiment. We want to fine tune this experiment. I see no point in trying to have five, six or seven other reports implemented without previous experimentation, if we saw it necessary to conduct an experiment on the third report before implementing it.
The fact that we are proroguing does not kill any report. There is no need for the reports to appear on any Order Paper. I challenge my hon. colleague to estimate the number of people who read the Order Paper every day. There are no consequences at all. However, to please the Opposition, we would not mind having those motions appear under Government business or under Government Orders in the new session. If they do not want that, fine, but they will not see them in the state they appear now under 200 notices of motions to concur. They are notices of obstruction, and this is totally unacceptable to the Government.

I know of no other Bill affecting the fisheries which has moved through the House so rapidly and with such thorough scrutiny by all interested parties.
A great deal has happened in a very short time. As Hon. Members know, this Bill received second reading on November 18. The industry, for its part, needs to look Government in the eye and make up its mind about its commitment and its intentions. You cannot legislate this kind of confidence, nor can you build it from a distance. You can, however, develop it through direct dialogue. I will not pretend that we have
